lead: A water tank must hold water without leaking, and that changes the design aim. A beam may crack finely and still be safe; a tank wall with the same cracks would weep. So tanks are designed to keep concrete tension low or crack widths tiny under the working load, with low steel stresses and small, closely spaced bars. Water pressure rises with depth, a circular wall resists it by hoop tension, and a rectangular wall resists it by bending. Overhead tanks, underground sumps and treatment tanks across Indian towns are designed this way, to IS 3370.
prereq: You need hydrostatic pressure and the working stress idea (see Working stress method and permissible stresses), and cantilever slab bending from Cantilever retaining walls.

sections.h3: Water pressure and the design aim

blocks.where: p is the water pressure in kN/m² at depth h (m) below the water surface; γ<sub>w</sub> is taken as 10 kN/m³ in design (9.81 kN/m³ for fresh water).

blocks.text: The pressure diagram on a wall is a triangle, zero at the surface and γ<sub>w</sub>H at the base. IS 3370 (Part 2):2009 limits the calculated crack width of liquid-retaining faces to 0.2 mm. It also gives a simpler route: crack widths are taken as acceptable if the steel stress at working load does not exceed 130 N/mm² for high-yield deformed bars (115 N/mm² for plain bars). For the walls to be uncracked, the concrete tensile stress is checked against limits such as 1.5 N/mm² in direct tension and 2.0 N/mm² in bending for M30.

Minimum steel in each direction is 0.35 % of the concrete section for deformed bars, reducible to 0.24 % for tanks with no dimension over 15 m. Bar spacing should not exceed 300 mm or the wall thickness. Walls thinner than 200 mm may have all their steel in one layer. Tanks need two load cases: full (water pushing out) and, for underground tanks, empty (soil and ground water pushing in, and uplift).

sections.h3: Circular tanks with a flexible base: hoop tension

blocks.text: Cut a 1 m high ring at depth h in half. The water pushes on the projected area 2r × 1 with force 2pr; the two cut faces pull back with 2T. So the ring tension is:
T = p r = γ<sub>w</sub> h r  (kN per metre height)
blocks.where: r is the internal radius in m. The hoop steel is A<sub>s</sub> = T/σ<sub>st</sub> with σ<sub>st</sub> = 130 N/mm²; the concrete check is T/(1000t + (m − 1)A<sub>s</sub>) ≤ σ<sub>ct</sub>, where t is the wall thickness in mm and m = 280/(3σ<sub>cbc</sub>) is the modular ratio (9.33 for M30, σ<sub>cbc</sub> = 10 N/mm²).

blocks.text: With a flexible (sliding) joint at the base, the wall carries pure hoop tension; the rings are heaviest at the bottom and can be reduced higher up. With a fixed base the wall also bends vertically near the bottom and needs vertical bars for that moment, from coefficient tables in IS 3370 (Part 4).

A long wall of a rectangular tank, fixed at the base and free at the top, is a vertical cantilever under triangular pressure: M = γ<sub>w</sub>H³/6 per metre at the base, with tension on the water face. Short walls span both ways between their neighbours and the base and are designed with plate coefficients. The base slab carries the water weight to the ground or, in an elevated tank, spans to the staging.

items: Use bars of 8 to 16 mm at 100 to 200 mm, lapped in a staggered pattern.
Use dense concrete of low water–cement ratio, cured well; M30 is the usual grade for liquid-retaining RC.
Seal construction joints with water bars; test the tank by filling it before finishes.

examples.question: A circular tank of 6 m internal diameter holds water 3.5 m deep and has a flexible base joint. Design the wall at the base in M30 concrete with Fe415 bars, using σ<sub>st</sub> = 130 N/mm² and σ<sub>ct</sub> = 1.5 N/mm².
steps: Pressure at the base: p = 10 × 3.5 = 35 kN/m². Hoop tension T = p r = 35 × 3 = 105 kN/m.
Hoop steel: A<sub>s</sub> = 105000/130 = 808 mm²/m. Provide 12 mm rings at 130 mm c/c: 870 mm²/m.
Thickness for no cracking: 105000/(1000t + 8.33 × 808) ≤ 1.5 gives t ≥ 63 mm. That is far less than practical; adopt t = 150 mm (a common rule is 30H + 50 = 155 mm, H in m).
Vertical steel: minimum 0.24 % of 1000 × 150 = 360 mm²/m (tank under 15 m); spacing not over 150 mm, so 8 mm at 130 mm c/c (387 mm²/m). With t < 200 mm both layers may be in one face.

Higher up: at 2.0 m depth (1.5 m below the top) T = 10 × 2.0 × 3 = 60 kN/m and A<sub>s</sub> = 462 mm²/m, so 12 mm rings could open to 245 mm, but they are limited by the 150 mm spacing rule to 150 mm (754 mm²/m).
examples.answer: Wall 150 mm thick; hoop steel 12 mm at 130 mm c/c at the base (870 mm²/m against 808); concrete tension 0.67 N/mm²; vertical 8 mm at 130 mm c/c.

traps: Using the diameter in T = pr. Use the radius.
Using the average pressure for the base ring. Each ring takes the pressure at its own depth.
Designing a tank wall at the limit state of collapse only. The working steel stress (130 N/mm²) or the 0.2 mm crack width governs.
Taking M = γ<sub>w</sub>H³/2 for a cantilever wall. Triangular load gives H³/6 (45 kN·m/m for 3 m), uniform load would give pH²/2.
Forgetting the empty-tank case of an underground sump: outside soil pressure and flotation.

quiz.q: What working steel stress does IS 3370 (Part 2):2009 accept for deformed bars in place of a crack-width calculation?
quiz.a: 130 N/mm² (115 N/mm² for plain bars); the crack-width limit itself is 0.2 mm.

quiz.q: Why is a circular wall cheaper than a rectangular wall for the same water depth?
quiz.a: The circular wall carries pressure as uniform hoop tension across its thickness; the rectangular wall must bend as a cantilever, which needs a thicker section and more steel for the same water.

quiz.q: A circular tank of 8 m diameter holds 4 m of water. Find T at the base and the hoop steel at 130 N/mm².
A rectangular tank wall 3 m high is fixed at the base and free at the top. Find the base moment per metre.
quiz.a: M = 10 × 3³/6 = 45 kN·m/m, tension on the water face.

quiz.q: In the worked example, could the wall be 120 mm thick?
quiz.a: Concrete: 105000/(120 000 + 8.33 × 870) = 0.83 N/mm², still below 1.5. But spacing must not exceed the thickness (120 mm) and cover of about 40 mm each side leaves little room for the bars and for compaction, so 150 mm is the practical minimum.

quiz.q: Why are small bars at close spacing preferred in tank walls?
quiz.a: For the same steel area, small bars at close spacing give more bar surface for bond, so cracks stay many and narrow rather than few and wide.

beyond: Not for the exam. Large circular tanks are often prestressed with wires wound round the wall, so the concrete stays in compression and never cracks (see Basic principles and advantages of prestressing). Elevated tanks are also checked for earthquakes with the sloshing water modelled as separate masses, as in IS 1893 (Part 2). Search for "Intze tank", "prestressed circular tank" and "IS 1893 part 2 liquid retaining tanks".

figure.caption: The worked example’s 6 m tank. Left: water 3.5 m deep presses on the 150 mm wall with a pressure that grows from zero to 35 kN/m² at the base. Right: a 1 m high ring at the base cut in half; the water pushes on 2r = 6 m and the two cut ends pull back with 2T, so T = pr = 105 kN/m, carried by 12 mm rings at 130 mm.
